economic globalisationó oõbrien and leichenko political ecologists developed this approach to understand the simultaneous effects of climate change and globalization on regions communities and ecosystems it exposes carbon credits as a doubleedged sword where excessive rain and droughts brought on by climate change intersect with a changing financial landscape in the globalized economy through trade liberalization and increased foreign investments vulnerable communities often lack the capacity to cope with this kind of double pressure and this usually leads to a worsening of their standard of living and increased economic vulnerabilities unless mitigated by targeted interventions evite and zara while carbon credits provide financial incentivization to local communities for maintaining rangelands swamps or forests to store more carbon and help mitigate climate change they have proven to pose potential risks of exacerbating resourcebased conflicts due to abrupt and largescale landuse changes and restriction policies that socially and economically affect local communities in marginalized regions thus critics of climate finance argue that it is a mechanism that promotes neocolonialism in the global south because it is an initiative funded by the global north evite and zara the argument is that the commodification of natural resources often through carbon credit schemes has led to unprecedented land use and ownership shifts this has exacerbated resourcebased conflicts in these regions as the authority over land has gone into the hands of private businesses at the frontier and out of the hands of the state bersaglio lohmann these disruptions affect traditional livelihoods and create dependency on profitoriented external markets from carbon creditsnorthern kenyas historical and current conflict dynamics todayõs northern kenya formerly known as the northern frontier district nfd was established during british colonial rule in it covers a vast area inhabited primarily by pastoralist communities throughout the colonial period the nfd was administered separately from the rest of the country a policy driven by its perceived remoteness and security concerns related to the regionõs proximity to ethiopia and somalia schlee following a failed attempt to join somalia after kenyaõs independence in the nfd has coped with a legacy of neglect marginalization and contested identity to date sharamo northern kenya has long been characterized by violent conflicts particularly among pastoral groups using the acled armed conflict location and event data to analyze pastoral conflicts in the last five years figure illustrates the fluctuation in lethal eventsñat least one person killed the number of conflict events involving pastoral actors and the resulting fatalities conflict incidents intensified and lethal conflicts also showed a substantial increase this is partly tied to the prolonged drought that affected northern kenya between to suggesting a correlation between environmentalinduced challenges that enhanced the mobility of pastoralists and intensifying conflicts over scarce resources the conflict also shows the postelection violence that affected the whole country traditional ethnic rivalries the need to restock livestock after drought or disease and cultural practices such as revenge supremacy battles and bride price payments continue to play a role witsenburg and adano more recent factors include boundarymaking conflicts caused by ethnically defined counties since devolution is pushing for defined county boundaries escalating ethnic mobilization and politicization of ethnicity these new dynamics combined with the commercialization of livestock rustling have intensified resource competition as fighting is focused on access and control and boundaries seem to be a tool that can enable access or limit one community against accessing resources across intercounty borderlands eaton schilling et al critical pastoral resources such as livestock water land and pasture are central to these conflicts these resources are all affected by environmental pressures including droughts floods and increasing variability in the regionõs two major rainy seasons april and october eberle et al in northern kenya while climaterelated resource scarcity such as the prolonged drought affects the timing and frequency of raids governance of these resources in the newly devolved system are critical in determining whether resource depletion leads to conflict or more cooperation with nrt through conservation initiatives conflicts intensified following conservancies expansion and commercialized raids it is involving local warriors and nrt rangers the ngo has been condemned by local communities as an agent of violence following the extrajudicial killings of local pastoralists even though the nrt promotes itself as an agent of peace by defining its work in conservation as peacebuilding counsell the environmental solution agenda lies a problematic complex of social inequalities and violent contestations stemming from restricted grazing policies and the exclusion of pastoralists from carbon financial benefits the reallocation of traditional communal grazing lands for carbon sequestration zones within borana and samburu land turned into a violent invasion in when young morans unmarried essential for their survival as resources were shared in times of severe environmental scarcity which has been disrupted by the carbon credit model of preserving rangelands for carbon storage in the pastoral livestock in northern kenya the need for pasture was urgent see the spike of conflicts from figure above the exclusion from these grazing lands was perceived as a loss of economic livelihood and a violation of customary land rights the situation worsened insecurity and often pushed the state to deploy police officers to protect tourist facilities from local invasions between when carbon funds were dispatched to conservancies and nrt spent more resources and time on peacebuilding activities following a spike of violence in conservancies rather than using those funds for pastoral development these areas are now converted to tourism sites with expensive lodges that locals cannot access or afford even for manual labor they are also defined as core conservation areas for wildlife blocking the pastoral communities this led to tensions among the locals who felt disenfranchised by the carbon project placing international markets over the wellbeing of the locals and the survival of their culture and livelihood for future generations as one of the elders representing the borana community in isiolo statedwe have a traditional system of managing rangeland known as the dedha using our name to get money and nothing comes to the communitymoreover inequalities have been exacerbated by the way carbon revenues are distributed as nrt and international partners like the nature conservancy benefit from carbon sales the local pastoralists reap limited or no financial rewards for instance nrt disclosed that in and each of the conservancies received us$ per conservancy from carbon sales ndirangu according to the nrt bylaws the funds should be directed through the conservancy managers who work with the board members to make decisions for the community regarding which projects or issues to focus resources on and support the conservancy members however the locals interviewed felt sidelined from the decisionmaking process resulting in increased mistrust frustration and suspicion about the true beneficiaries of carbon funds the pastoralists interviewed claimed that the process is topdown and institutionalized fearing there is no transparency in what nrt gets from the òsale of their airó interviewees also pointed to systemic issues within conservancies as unequal distribution of carbon revenues reinforces existing social hierarchies because elites closely supported by politicians and economic power structures benefit disproportionately from carbon credit sales it was noted that some board members and managers are accused of mismanaging funds and there are reports of political interference and manipulation during elections for conservancy chairpersons making it a lucrative position to die for this is because elites often control resources channeled to manage development within conservancies they allegedly use their positions power and influence for personal gain excluding the broader community from the benefits the sidelining of pastoralist voices fuels resentment and perpetuates further marginalization in a region grappling with historical neglect policies stemming from colonial and postcolonial regimes that have not been addressed to date ethnic rivalries governance challenges and limited access to development further complicate these resourcebased conflicts according to survival international blood carbon report of the nkrcp project design should have considered the indigenous knowledge systems and priorities of pastoralists who own land and resources locals also affirmed this during the interviews some respondents felt that the promise of longterm environmental sustainability through carbon credits was too abstract for local needs and realities these specifically stemmed from grazing committees and councils of elders unaware of where the carbon revenues disappeared after being released by nrt to the conservancy managers many stated that they are left in the dark as no one has ever called for a public participation meeting per the kenyan constitution to decide on projects appropriate for pastoralists as few elites decide on their behalf what they think is best for the community another significant issue concerning the concept of the carbon project is the gap in understanding about what carbon is and how it is measured how it operates and where it is sold pastoralists interviewed could not fully grasp the concept of carbon trading to them they know nrt is òselling their airó or òsuwoó as the samburu call it this has led to confusion rumors and mistrust as some were skeptical of taking the money alluding to it as dirtyblood money because selling air is like selling ghosts some communities also acknowledged receiving benefits such as scholarships and bursaries for their children water projects and employment of rangers in conservancies however the general sentiment is that these benefits are unevenly distributed throughout northern kenya which is conserving its rangelands the issue of corruption and emerging carbon millionaires who are conservancy managers is becoming a concern the perception is that a significant amount of money is being funneled into private hands rather than shared equitably by the communities doing the rangeland management work when carbon was implemented the pastoral communities had higher expectations and aspirations hoping to improve their livelihoods although the project was initially perceived as a potential source of wealth and development the reality has disappointed many pastoralistsconclusion the surge of capitalist naturebased solution projects such as carbon credits poses a risk of escalating natural resource conflicts especially in the global south where rangelands forests and swamps are targeted and converted in the name of invasive and expansive activities such as carbon offset schemes weldemichel the findings reveal that climate finance initiatives such as carbon markets offer new economic opportunities to empower indigenous communities livelihoods they have proven that they also limit control access and use of critical resources like rangelands for pastoralist groups in northern kenya this complicates traditional resourcesharing mechanisms by the pastoral communities whose ethnic or county boundaries have never been delimited the carbon project poses the risk of dispossession of pastoralists from their ancestral lands amplifying resource competition by creating scarcity in fragile ecologies prone to climate variabilities several communities had to alter traditional grazing patterns due to climate variability and newly imposed land management policies under the carbon sequestration project promoted by nrt for communities that have faced marginalization and underdevelopment for decades from colonial to postcolonial regimes in kenya the carbon project is seen as another form of invasion and alienation of indigenous landexternal entrepreneurs impose carbon credit interventions that do not serve pastoralistsõ interests nor address their urgent realities and needs the entanglement of harsh environmental changes natural resource exploitation and restrictions and social inequalities intensifies competition over shrinking resources these communities are already locked in ethnic rivalries and resourcebased conflicts they are now experiencing the new dilemma of greater polarization as restrictions on land are viewed through the lens of carbon colonialism additionally the intensification and expansion of conservation efforts in northern kenya continue to pose further challenges produced by international actorsõ capitalistdriven motives the lack of genuine community involvement the missing action of the kenya government in protecting the vulnerable communities the inadequate devolution of conservation landscapes and ongoing resource conflicts these issues undermine carbon marketsõ professed sustainable environment wildlife conservation and equitable and sustainable development goals the findings have shown that the nkrcp exemplifies a double exposure tragedy in that pastoral communities grapple with the doubleedged frontier of climateinduced environmental changes and the commodification of capitalist appropriation of natural resources
